opener.heading: Week 22: Memorial Day & Community Heroes 🎖️
about: This week runs on people. Azlyn draws her own street down the middle of the living room floor and marks a door into every house for you to cut, tapes the whole family up on a door in rows, with the lines between them showing, and carries a jar of cookie mix across the road to a neighbor. She stocks a box of water by the front door for whoever knocks, runs Kreston's entire morning on Tuesday while you sit on your hands, and takes a phone round the house showing her bed to somebody hundreds of miles off. Each day puts the same question in front of her in a new shape: who is around us, and what do we do for them?

Memorial Day lands on Monday the 31st, and Day 151 takes it at three-year-old size. One person named out loud, three small true stories from before she was born, and a windowsill cleared for a photograph, a jar of picked flowers and one object that person used to hold. Four things outlast the seven days: the street map, the family cards on the door, the water box on the step and the remembering shelf. Leave the shelf up longest. She will walk past it for weeks and ask about it at odd moments, which is why it goes at her height and not on top of the bookcase.
azlyn: Her street has a shape she can draw. Two long lines for road and sidewalk, houses in a row along her side, then the real doors counted against her map on the walk.
Everybody carries more than one name. Joseph is your dad, Kreston's dad and grandma's son, and the cards taped up in rows put those lines where she can point at them.
Layering by hand. Flour, two sugars, oats and raisins tapped flat one at a time into a jar, tablespoon for the bulk and teaspoon for the last of it.
Doing something for a person who is not in the room. A box she loads herself, somebody else's flowers watered, and two bottles missing by teatime as the evidence.
People were here before she was. Three objects older than her, three stories from then, and one shelf given over to somebody who is gone.
you: Outdoor time is doing more than you can see

Secrets are cognitively demanding, and she will probably fail
Children can't yet imagine their parents as separate people
Acts of service are the hardest gift for a young child to conceive of
Video calls are hard for young children, and that's not rudeness
Children don't have autobiographical memory the way we assume

Thin card, about 30 pieces (4 or 5 cereal boxes cut into panels)
Thick card, 1 sheet, for the handprints
A large envelope, or a cereal box to fold into one
Brown paper, or a paper bag cut open flat
A craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
A ruler, or a straight strip of card
A clean jar with a lid, big enough for three cups of dry ingredients
A clean jam jar with a lid, for the flowers on the sill
A small funnel, or paper to fold one
A banana or a cucumber, cut into strips Kreston can hold
Small toy figures, or clothespins, 10 (two of them get faces on Wednesday)
A cloth for wiping the windowsill
A trash bag, or a plastic bag
Kreston's bib, his cup and one board book
Every printed photograph in the house, the 2–3 oldest included
Three things older than Azlyn, one of them the oldest thing you own
One object that belonged to the person you are remembering
A photograph of their room, texted over before Wednesday
A mug and a hardback book, to prop the phone at her height
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 11 months this week. He lets go of the furniture and stands on his own for a second or two before he sits down, pulls up on anything at chest height, and babbles at length in a voice that rises and falls like talking. He turns one on Saturday the 5th, two days after this week closes.

days.title: Who Comes to Our Street
days.prepTonight: Flatten two or three boxes down the living room floor with the crayons and the tape on top, and dig out any printed family photographs for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Walking the Street with One Finger

opening.title: The Doorstep List
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the front doorstep.
steps: Sit on the step and write down everybody who comes to this street in a week. Post, bins, deliveries, the meter reader, the neighbor with the dog.
She adds to it. Take everything, including the cat and the people who came once in March.
Tell her the street gets built on the living room floor at 9:15, and this list decides who walks down it.

main.title: The Street on the Floor
materials: 2–3 flattened cardboard boxes, or a length of lining paper
A ruler or a straight strip of card
Small toy figures, or clothespins, as the people
steps: Tape the cardboard into one long strip down the middle of the floor, joins underneath.
Give her the ruler and a crayon and run two long lines the length of it: road in the middle, sidewalk each side.
Count the houses out loud at the window, then let her draw them along her side. Start with your own so she has something to count from.
Every house gets a door and a number. She says which number goes where and you write them in marker.
Add the rest of the doorstep list. The mailbox, the lamppost, the trash cans on their day, the corner store.
Stand the figures on the road as the people. Leave it down, because the doors get cut this afternoon.
main.tip: Her street will have the store next door and your house in the middle of the road. Leave it. Correcting the map costs you the rest of the hour.

outside.title: Buttercups Under Chins
paras: Walk the stretch of sidewalk she drew this morning and count the real doors against her drawing. Find the buttercups on the roadside or the edge of the green and hold one under her chin. Yellow means she likes butter, which has never been true and has never stopped anybody. Pick a few for the windowsill, out of mouths on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and lets go of the furniture for a second before he sits down again. Give him the far end of the cardboard, past where Azlyn is working, and a fat crayon of his own. On the walk, let him push the empty stroller for the last stretch.

second.title: The Doors That Open
second.intro: Every front door on the map gets a hinge this afternoon, and somebody moves in behind it.
materials: The street map from this morning
The doorstep list from this morning
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Thin card, 6–8 pieces, for the people
steps: Go house to house. She draws a crayon line down the hinge side of each door, and that side stays uncut.
Cut the other three sides yourself with her sat back on the sofa. The knife goes up on the shelf between houses.
Fold every door open and shut a few times so it stays where she puts it.
Thin card next. She draws one person per door, small enough to stand behind it, and you write the name she gives them.
Tape each person behind their own door, on a strip of tape folded into a stand so they hold upright.
Now knock. You tap a door, she opens it and says who lives there. Go up the street and back down.
Draw the visitors from the doorstep list on the last two cards and walk them along the road, stopping at the right houses.
second.tip: Let her decide who lives where. The neighbor's dog will end up in your house and the mailman at number four.

alternatives: One door, one person, and the rest of the map left plain.
Post scraps of paper through the finished doors and fish them out.
Chalk the street on the sidewalk instead, at full size.
Photograph every front door and match the photos to her drawings.
outAgain: The café, a window seat, one cake between you and an hour of watching who goes past
The park, for the swings and nothing else
A friend's house, if anyone is free on a Friday
The corner store, and let her hand the money over
The same walk again, counting which doors have somebody home

aroundWorld.title: Remembering, Everywhere 🎖️
paras: Every country keeps its dead somewhere. In Japan, families clean the graves in August for Obon, hang lanterns to light the way home, then float those lanterns down a river to send them back. In Mexico, Día de los Muertos puts marigolds and the person's own favorite meal out on a table at home. Across the Netherlands, everything stops at eight in the evening on May 4 for two minutes of silence, buses and trains included.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Cook one thing the person you are remembering liked to eat, and say whose dinner it is before anyone picks up a fork. Azlyn will ask for it again next year, which is how a recipe carries a person.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Marigolds are used because the smell is strong enough to be followed.

days.krestonPM: He comes to the café in the high chair with a crust and a spoon. At 11 months a room of strangers is work, and he does it by watching one person at a time. Say the words for whatever he points at.

insight.headline: Outdoor time is doing more than you can see.
paras: You get her out twice a day because it burns off the noise. Daylight is also working on the inside of her eyes. Time outdoors has one of the strongest protective links we know of to short-sightedness in children, and the effect seems to come from the light level and from looking at things far away rather than from anything she does out there. A cloudy May morning still throws ten times the light of a lit kitchen. Two hours a day is the figure that keeps coming up, and between the walk and the hour out again you are most of the way there.

days.safety: The craft knife is adult-only and goes back out of reach between cuts, on a shelf and not the arm of the sofa. Kreston is 11 months, pulls up on the table edge and mouths whatever he lands on, so the card offcuts and the small paper people come off the floor before he is put down. The toy figures or clothespins standing on the road come up with them.

days.title: Everyone in the Family
days.prepTonight: Cut ten or twelve rectangles out of cereal boxes, stack them by the door with the crayons and the photographs, and wash the big jar and its lid for tomorrow.

opening.title: Spreading Out the Photographs
opening.need: every printed photograph in the house · the kitchen table, cleared.
steps: Spread them face up across the whole table. If they all live on your phone, pick ten and go one at a time.
She names who she can. You name the rest, and say the relationship with the name: that is Joseph's mom, so she is your grandma.
Count the people the family has. She will land on a different number every time, so take the last one and tell her they each get a card at 9:15.

main.title: Who Belongs to Who
materials: Card or cereal-box panels cut into 10–12 rectangles
Printed photos if you have any, otherwise she draws each face
A door or a blank stretch of wall
steps: Start at the bottom, at her eye height. Azlyn and Kreston, one card each. She draws the faces, you write the names in marker.
Row above: you and Joseph. Say it while you tape. I am your mom, Joseph is your dad, and we are Kreston's mom and dad as well.
Row above that: grandparents. Tape a photograph onto the card where you have one, and she draws the ones you do not.
Run a strip of masking tape from each parent down to each of their children, so the lines are there to point at.
Aunts, uncles and cousins go out to the sides at the height that matches their row. Give the dog a card if she asks.
Stand back and ask questions the wall can answer. Who is Kreston's dad. Who is grandma's daughter. Leave it up all week.
main.tip: Say the relationship every time you say a name today, even when it sounds laboured. She hears grandma as a name, the way she hears Kreston.

outside.title: A Daisy for Each Person
paras: Late May and the daisies are thick on any grass that has not been cut this week. Give her one job: one daisy for every person on the door. She will lose count and start again twice. Sit down when the bunch looks about right, count it against the names, and split the chain-making between you on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and knows the faces in this house before anything else in it. Hold his own card up and say his name, then Azlyn's, and watch him reach for the face he knows. Out on the grass, sit him in the daisies and let him pull to standing off your knee to get at them.

second.title: Finding Everybody Again
second.intro: The cards come off the door after lunch and go round the house, and she has to earn every one of them back.
materials: A basket or a paper bag for carrying finds
A cushion for Kreston's spot on the floor
steps: Send her upstairs to count to twenty. Hide the cards one per room, at her height, nothing above her reach.
Hand her the basket with one rule: she names who it is and who they belong to before it goes in.
When she stalls, give her the relationship instead of the name. This one is Joseph's mom. She gets there from that.
Sit Kreston on the cushion where he can watch, and lay the full basket out in rows on the table, above his reach.
She tapes them back up herself, in whatever order she wants, which will not be this morning's.
Play the swap. She shuts her eyes, you take one card down, and she works out who is missing from the gap.
Last round is hers. She hides them, you hunt, and you name the wrong person on purpose at least twice.
second.tip: Naming who is missing is harder than naming who is there, so hold step six back until she has won a few of the easy rounds.

alternatives: Hide three cards instead of twelve and stop when she has them.
Sort the cards into who lives in this house and who does not.
Mail the cards through the doors on yesterday's street map.
Draw one more card for somebody she has thought of since breakfast.
outAgain: A bus ride to nowhere in particular, upstairs at the front, home on the next one
The park, if the bus feels like too much organizing
A walk to the mailbox with a card she has drawn for somebody on the wall
Any bench with a view of a busy road
Grandparents, if anyone on the door is close enough to call in on
days.krestonPM: Take him on the bus in the sling and stand him on your knee at the window. At 11 months he tracks what moves past him and turns back to check your face, which is him asking whether the truck was worth reacting to. Answer him, and let Azlyn ring the bell.

insight.headline: Family structure is confusing at three, and worth being explicit about.
paras: Azlyn hears grandma as a name, the way she hears Kreston. Understanding that one person carries several labels at once, that Joseph is your dad and also Kreston's dad and also somebody's son, takes relational thinking that arrives closer to five or six. Until then she files people one label deep. Saying the relationship whenever you say a name, and putting the cards in rows where the lines between them show, hands her the structure in a form she can point at. She will get it wrong for another two years. The version she builds now is the one that gets corrected, and it has to exist first.

days.safety: The cards and the masking tape stay off the floor while Kreston is down. He is 11 months, pulls up on the table edge and mouths whatever he lands on, and a cereal-box card is the right size to go in a mouth. Hide the cards at her height and nowhere she has to climb for.

days.title: The Secret She Can't Keep
days.prepTonight: Stand the washed jar on the table with the flour, both sugars, the oats and the raisins, and decide tonight which person tomorrow's shelf is for.

opening.title: Picking the Person
steps: Ask her who outside this house has been kind to her this week. Offer names if she stalls: the neighbor, the woman in the store, whoever brings the mail.
She draws them. You write the name across the top.
Say the rule once. It is a surprise until we hand it over. Then let her practice telling you what is in it.

main.title: The Jar That Bakes Later
materials: 1 clean jar with a lid, big enough for three cups of dry ingredients
White sugar and brown sugar, 1/3 cup each
steps: Jar on the table, funnel in the neck. Flour first, tablespoon for the bulk and teaspoon for the last of it. She taps it flat with the back of the spoon.
White sugar next, then brown sugar pressed down hard so the line between them stays sharp.
Oats after that, tapped down the same way. Raisins or chocolate chips last, up to the neck of the jar so nothing shifts on the walk over.
Lid on tight, and the jar goes high on a shelf while she does the label.
She draws on one side of the card. On the other you write the method: tip into a bowl, add a stick of soft butter and one egg, roll into balls, twelve minutes at 350 degrees. Sign it from Azlyn.
Tie the string twice round the neck, tuck the label under it, and let her pull the knot tight with you.
main.tip: Flat layers make it a gift instead of a bag of groceries. Let her do the tapping and accept the mess.

outside.title: First Barefoot Grass
paras: Pick the warmest part of the day and take everybody's shoes off on grass for the first time this year. She will stand on the spot before she trusts it. Walk her across the whole patch: the cold strip in the shade of the hedge, the dry prickle where the sun has had it all morning, the give underneath after a wet week.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a second or two on a flat floor. Set him down barefoot on grass and he will hold one foot up, curl his toes and object at the texture before he agrees to weight it. Hold his hands and wait him out.

second.title: Delivering It Without Telling
second.intro: The jar goes across the road this afternoon, wrapped in paper she has covered herself.
materials: Brown paper, or a paper bag cut open flat
steps: Spread the brown paper on the floor and give her the crayons. Whole sheet, ten solid minutes.
Move to the table for the jar. Paper up round the glass, tape wherever she is holding it. Lumpy is the correct result.
Message card: she draws, and underneath you write what she dictates, word for word.
String round the parcel, card tucked under the string, knot pulled tight by both of you.
Rehearse on the way over. Give her one sentence for the door and let her change it.
She carries it with both hands and she knocks. Stand a pace back.
She will announce what is inside before the door is halfway open. Let her, and let the neighbor do the surprised face.
second.tip: Do not prompt her on the doorstep. A three-year-old fed her line in front of a stranger goes silent.

alternatives: Wrap it in a paper bag with one drawing taped on and go.
Mail the message card today and hand the jar over tomorrow.
Fill a second jar for somebody in this house instead.
Draw the neighbor's front door and add it to Friday's street map.
outAgain: A playground you have never been to, two streets past the usual one
The long way home from the delivery, on the other side of the road
Feeding the ducks, if the new playground is too far
A field, a ball and nothing organized
The same barefoot grass again, with a blanket and a book
days.krestonPM: New playground, new bars to pull up on. At 11 months he wants the equipment the big children are on, so let him watch the baby swing from your arms first, then put him in it. Push him facing Azlyn, because he checks where she is every twenty seconds.

insight.headline: Secrets are cognitively demanding, and she will probably fail.
paras: Holding a surprise asks two hard things of her at once. She has to track what somebody else does not know, which is theory of mind and still under construction at three, and she has to stop herself saying the most exciting thing in her head, which is inhibitory control and thinner now than it ever will be. Most three-year-olds leak the surprise inside a minute of meeting the person. Set the day up so the telling is the gift: she carries the parcel, she knocks, she announces what is in it on the doorstep. Nobody has to pretend, and she gets the practice without the failure.

days.safety: A glass jar at floor level with an 11-month-old who stands and cruises. Fill it and wrap it on the table, never on the floor, and put it high the moment the lid is on. Loose oats, raisins and chocolate chips are all choking-sized for Kreston, so sweep before he goes down. You carry the jar over the road and hand it to her on the far curb, so the crossing happens with your hands on the glass.

days.title: Before Azlyn
days.prepTonight: Stand three things older than Azlyn on the kitchen counter, the oldest thing in the house among them, put the two or three oldest photographs out of her reach with one small thing that belonged to the person you chose, and count the small water bottles for Tuesday.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Story She Asks For Again

opening.title: Older Than Her
opening.need: 3 things older than Azlyn, one of them the oldest thing in the house · the kitchen table.
steps: Line the three up on the table and let her handle all of them.
Ask which is oldest. Take her guess, then tell her the real age of each one and where it came from.
Every object on this table was here before she was. Say that out loud, and tell her three stories from then are coming at 9:15.

main.title: Three Stories from Before
materials: 1 marker, for you to write the caption she gives each drawing
steps: Paper and crayons down in front of her, then start talking. She draws while you talk.
Story one is yours, from before she was born. Keep it small and true: the job you hated, the apartment with the broken window, the first time you met Joseph.
Story two is Joseph's. Pick one he tells at the table, or ring him and let him tell it himself.
Story three is the person who is gone, with the old photograph out. Say the name, say how you are related, and say one thing they did that you can still see them doing.
Ask her what each story was about as she finishes each drawing and write her answer on it. She will get it wrong, and the wrong version is worth keeping.
Tape the three drawings in a row above the windowsill you are clearing at 1:00.
main.tip: Story three does its work with no ceremony attached. Tell the sad one the way you told the funny one. She reads your face first, and a warm flat delivery lets her ask questions.

outside.title: A Bunch for the Photograph
paras: Go out with one purpose: enough flowers for a jam jar on a windowsill. Late May puts them everywhere, buttercups and clover on the green, wild mustard along the roadside, whatever has escaped a garden wall. She picks and she decides. If your town has a memorial, walk past it. There will be flowers on it today, put there by somebody this morning.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and has started handing things over on purpose. Give him one sturdy stalk and hold your hand out for it. He gives it, takes it back and gives it again, twenty times over. Keep the picked flowers out of his mouth walking home.

second.title: The Remembering Shelf
second.intro: One windowsill becomes a place for one person this afternoon, and it stays that way well past this week.
materials: A windowsill or a low shelf, cleared
1 small jar or glass of water
One object that belonged to the person
Card and a marker for the name
A cloth for wiping the sill
steps: She clears the sill herself and wipes it with the cloth. Everything that used to live there goes elsewhere.
Fill the jar at the tap and let her carry it the whole way, both hands, at whatever speed she manages.
She snaps the stems short with her fingers and puts the flowers in. Crowded and lopsided is fine.
The photograph goes at the back, propped against the glass. She picks which one faces into the room.
The object goes in front. Tell her whose hands used it and what for, and let her hold it before it goes down.
Name card last. She draws on it, you write the name in letters readable from the door, and it props against the jar.
Sit down in front of the lot before you tidy anything. Ask her to tell one of the three stories back. Take whatever version comes.
second.tip: Leave the shelf up. She will walk past it for weeks and ask about it at odd moments.

alternatives: One photograph and one jar of flowers, and stop there.
Draw the person from the photograph and tape it above the sill.
Ring the oldest person in the family and let her ask one question.
Go through a whole album on the floor and stop there.
outAgain: A field walk, the long edge of one, out and back, grass high enough to run a hand through
The riverside path, if the field is still wet from last week
A quiet stretch of the churchyard, walked slow
The green space with a ball, busier than usual with everybody off for Memorial Day
The playground, and let her run the whole hour off
days.krestonPM: Put him down where the grass is short and let him crawl. At 11 months he will sit and pull at one stalk for two minutes. Keep him off the roadside itself and carry him the last stretch.

insight.headline: Children can't yet imagine their parents as separate people.
paras: To Azlyn, you began when she did. She has no working model of you as a person with a childhood, a job you hated, an apartment with a broken window. Parents turn up in a three-year-old's mind as roles rather than histories, and the idea that you existed for years without her is close to unthinkable. One small true story from before she was born is the first evidence against that. She will not grasp it today. The shape is what stays: people were here before, some are gone, and the ones still here carry the stories. That is as much as a remembering day asks.

days.safety: You check every stem before she picks it. Poison hemlock grows along these roadsides, lacy white heads on a purple-blotched stem, and it is deadly. Nothing tall, white and lacy gets picked, nothing goes near a mouth, and hands get washed the moment you are in. The jar on the sill is glass. Stand it at the back of the sill, out of Kreston's reach, because he is 11 months and pulls up on anything at chest height.

days.title: Azlyn Runs the Morning
days.prepTonight: Clear Kreston's clothes drawer down to what he can wear, stand the shoebox and the water bottles by the front door, and text whoever you are calling on Wednesday for a photograph of their room.

schedule.name: The Jobs Done Before She Woke Up

opening.title: The Jobs Done Before She Woke Up
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the downstairs as you left it.
steps: Walk her round and hunt for what has already happened this morning. Kettle, dishwasher, curtains, bins out, Kreston fed and changed.
Write each one down as she spots it and let her mark it off.
Ask who did all of it. Then tell her Kreston's next hour is hers, and you are there for the lifting.

main.title: Azlyn Does Kreston's Morning
materials: His cup, for her to fill
Banana or cucumber cut into strips he can hold
A basket for his three chosen toys
steps: Clothes first. She picks the whole outfit out of the drawer and you put it on him without editing one item.
Bib next, and she does the fastening at the back of his neck. He wriggles.
Cup: she fills it at the tap, carries it over and hands it to him.
Snack: three strips onto his tray from her hand, and more when those have gone.
Washcloth over his face and hands at the end. He will object, she does it anyway.
Three toys into the basket, chosen by her, and that is his lot until lunch. Then she reads him the board book. He will crawl off halfway, and it counts as read.
main.tip: Sit on your hands unless he is about to fall. Every choice you correct tells her the job was never hers.

outside.title: Watering Somebody Else's Flowers
paras: June and the first dry spell, so take a full watering can up the road and water somebody else's pots. The neighbor who is at work, the tubs outside the store, the planter at the end of the street that nobody owns. She is doing a job for people who will never know it happened.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and follows more one-step instructions than he can answer. Hand him his cup and say drink, and watch him do it. He has spent the morning being served by his sister rather than by you. He will look for her when he wants something.

second.title: The Cold Water Box by the Door
second.intro: A box goes out by the front door this afternoon, stocked for whoever turns up.
materials: Card and crayons for the sign
A trash bag or plastic bag to keep the rain off
steps: Sit on the doorstep and count who comes to this door in a day and gets nothing out of it. The mail, deliveries, the trash collectors.
She loads the box: bottles along the bottom, snacks on top, in whatever order she decides.
Sign next. She draws on the card and you write underneath in marker what she dictates, big enough to read from the gate.
Tape the sign to the front of the box so it faces the path rather than the house.
Lay the trash bag over the top and tape the corners down at the back, so a shower does not turn the sign to mush.
She carries it out and picks the spot. Wherever she picks is where it goes.
Check it together at five and count what is left.
second.tip: Refill it before she is up and say nothing. Let her find it fuller than she left it.

alternatives: One bottle and one note taped to the door.
Draw the sign only, and load the box tomorrow.
A second box for the sidewalk outside the store.
Do the whole thing for the trash collectors, out on trash day.
outAgain: Swimming, and warm enough now to walk home with wet hair
The splash pad or the kiddie pool, if the session is full
A shallow bit of the river or the lake, feet only
The park with a picnic, if nobody can face changing rooms
The garden with a dishpan of water and two cups
days.krestonPM: He comes in with you. At 11 months he stands alone on land and has no idea that does not carry into water, so he stays in your hands. Walk him along the wall under the arms so he can pat it. Twenty minutes, then out.

insight.headline: Acts of service are the hardest gift for a young child to conceive of.
paras: Handing over a wrapped object is easy for her to understand. The thing was hers, then it was theirs, and she watched it happen. Doing something for a person who is not in the room asks her to hold a stranger in her head and picture them thirsty, a bigger act of imagination than most adults credit at three. Making the service concrete closes the gap: a box she can see, things she can count, a spot she chose, and two bottles missing from it by teatime. She takes generosity from the evidence, and the evidence today is the empty space in the box.

days.safety: Swimming with two children and one adult. Kreston is 11 months, stands alone for a moment and lunges at water, so he is in your hands the whole time and Azlyn stays inside arm's reach. Get him out at twenty minutes, hot day or not. Nothing goes in the water box that Kreston can reach if he is out on the step with you.

days.title: The People Who Are Far Away
days.prepTonight: Fix the call for mid-morning, charge the phone, check their photograph has arrived, and put May's drawings and pressed flowers in one pile for tomorrow.

schedule.name: The Call with Jobs In It

opening.title: Who Isn't Here
opening.need: the family cards from Saturday, still on the door · 1 sheet of paper · crayons.
steps: Go along the rows and ask which of these people she has not seen for a long time. Take her first answer.
Take that card off the door and let her carry it about.
She draws them a picture. Tell her it goes up on the screen at 9:15.

main.title: The Call with Jobs In It
materials: A mug and a book to prop it up at her height
One of the family cards from Saturday
steps: Give her the running order before you dial. Say hello, show the drawing, take them round the house, fetch Kreston, finish with the flashlight.
Prop the phone against the book with the mug behind it, down at her height, so nobody has to hold it up for ten minutes.
Hello and the drawing first, close enough to fill the screen. She will hold it upside down and explain it anyway.
Then the tour. She carries the phone round and shows them her bed, the window, and their own card, the one that came off the door this morning.
Fetch Kreston into shot and let her introduce him. She will lift his hand and wave it for him.
Finish with the flashlight. Big light off, flashlight under her chin, and the person on the screen does it back if they can find one.
main.tip: Let the silences run. The temptation is to fill every gap for both ends, and the call gets better once she works out nobody is going to talk over her.

outside.title: Finding the Elderflower
paras: Early June is the two weeks the elderberry is out, flat white plates of flower on a scruffy shrub along ditches, fence lines and the edge of any damp scrub. Walk until she finds one, check it yourself, then hold the head down for her to smell. It smells of honey with something sharper under it. Snap one head off for the sill and carry it yourself. If nothing is open yet, the black locust hanging in white chains over the road does the same job for her nose.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and knows voices with no face attached. Hold him in shot and watch him check behind the phone for the person. Hand him a board book once he has had his turn.

second.title: Their Room and Ours
second.intro: Two shoeboxes go down on the floor a hand's width apart, standing in for two rooms and the distance between them.
materials: 2 heavy books, to hold the boxes still
Scraps of card and an old dish towel for furniture
2 small dolls, or 2 clothespins with faces drawn on
2 short cardboard tubes as the phones
A photo of their room on your phone
steps: Lay both boxes on their sides, open faces toward each other, and weight each one with a book so they hold still.
The left box is theirs. Look at the photograph and copy it: wall color in crayon, a bed folded out of card, the dish towel as the blanket, a window drawn on the back panel.
The right box is hers, and she does it on her own. Hands off unless she asks.
Two clothespins or two dolls, faces drawn on in marker. One into each room, and she says which is which.
A cardboard tube in each room as the phone. Hold yours to your ear, she holds hers, and talk across the gap.
Run this morning's call again through the tubes. Hello, the drawing, the tour, then Kreston.
Lift the book off her box and slide it across the room, as far from theirs as the floor allows, then do the tube call from there.
second.tip: Copy their room down to the boring details, the lamp and the wrong-colored curtains.

alternatives: One box, their room only, and hers stays real.
Draw both rooms flat on one big sheet instead.
Record a video message and let her direct it.
Post a real letter with this morning's drawing folded inside.
outAgain: The church hall playgroup, and let her take one thing to show
Indoor playground, if the hall is shut for the holiday
The park with whoever is going
A walk to the mailbox with the letter
The garden center café, for a bun and a sit down
days.krestonPM: Playgroup at 11 months is a room of children who move faster than he does, and he will sit in the middle and watch. Put him down near the ride-on toys rather than the baby mat. He pulls up on anything at chest height.

insight.headline: Video calls are hard for young children, and that's not rudeness.
paras: Researchers call it the video deficit. Children under about three take in less from a screen than from the same person in the room, and the gap closes when the person on screen responds to them in real time. A face saying hello sweetheart on a loop gives her nothing to work with. A person who asks to see her bed, then waits while she carries the phone there, is running a live back-and-forth, and that she can use. Her wandering off mid-call is her going to find something to do. Build the call out of jobs and you answer that before it starts.

days.safety: Nothing picked on this walk goes near a mouth. Elderberry grows in the same rough ground as poison hemlock and water hemlock, both deadly and both carrying lacy white flower heads at this time of year, so you identify every plant before she touches it. Kreston is 11 months and mouths whatever reaches his hand, so he carries nothing and she hands everything to you. Wash both pairs of hands when you get in.

days.title: What We Keep
days.prepTonight: Scroll your phone back to Friday so this week's photographs are in order, and stand the paint, the brush, the card and a washcloth by the sink.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Reading the Week Back to Joseph

opening.title: Telling the Week Back
opening.need: your phone, with this week's photographs · the sofa.
steps: Sit down together and go through the week from Friday forward, in order, saying nothing.
She tells you what each one was. Let the order come out wrong and leave it wrong.
Count the days off on her fingers. Seven. Tell her each one gets its own card at 9:15.

main.title: The Week in Seven Pictures
materials: 1 marker, for writing her words down exactly as she says them
This week's photos on your phone
steps: Lay the seven cards in a row across the table. Put a finger on the first and say Friday.
Show her Friday's photo, then take the phone away before she picks up a crayon.
Ask what it is when she stops. Write her answer underneath in marker, word for word, wrong words and all.
Work along the row. Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Today goes last, and she decides what today has been.
Tape the seven up in a line at her height, beside the family cards on the door.
Walk the line and read her own words back in order. She will correct you on at least one, and her correction goes on the card.
main.tip: If four of the seven come out the same scribble, tape all four up. The words underneath are what you read next year.

outside.title: The Same Walk, All Green
paras: Walk the route you walked on the first day of January, when the trees were bare. It has closed over. Stop where January's photograph was taken, look up at a ceiling of leaves where there was sky in winter, and take the summer one from the same spot. Do four of these across the year, and keep them together.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and did this walk in January facing out of the carrier. Put him down at the flat stretch and let him walk it holding one finger. He turns twelve months on Saturday, so say happy nearly-one to him out there.

second.title: Sealing Up May
second.intro: May gets sealed into an envelope this afternoon, and June opens with fresh handprints.
materials: 1 large envelope, or a cereal box flattened and folded into one
The month's drawings and pressed flowers
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
Thick card, 1 sheet, for the handprints
steps: Spread May's drawings and pressed flowers over the floor. She keeps three out for the wall and the rest go in the envelope.
Write MAY and the year across the front, hand her the marker for the rest of it, then fold the flap over and press it down.

Handprints, and Kreston goes first while he is calm, washcloth already in your other hand. Paint his palm with the brush rather than dipping his hand, press flat on the card, lift straight up and wipe him down.
Azlyn next, her palm on the same sheet beside his. Same brush, press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write June, her 3 and his 11 months beside the pair of them.
Wash both pairs of hands and stand the card flat somewhere high to dry.
Growth chart: both of them against the door frame. Mark with the pencil, write the name and the date, and do the adults too.
Stand her next to May's mark and let her find the gap with her own finger. Ask what she thinks July will be and put a pencil dot there.
second.tip: Her guess will be near the ceiling. Put the dot where she says and leave it.

alternatives: Handprints only, and seal the envelope tomorrow.
Draw round both their hands in pencil instead.
Sort May's drawings into keep and send, and post two of them.
Measure everybody with string and tape the strings up.
outAgain: The thrift store, where she has a dollar and full authority over it
The park on the way back, to try whatever she came home with
The library, if the thrift store is shut by three
A bench outside the bakery, one bun, split four ways
The green space and a ball, if the store lasted four minutes
days.krestonPM: Thrift stores are the right size for an 11-month-old. Keep him in the sling and put him down in the book corner if there is one. Let Azlyn pick something for him and pay for it at the register. Nothing with a loose eye or a small wheel.

insight.headline: Children don't have autobiographical memory the way we assume.
paras: Azlyn will keep almost nothing from this week on her own. Autobiographical memory, the kind with a when and a who in it, assembles between three and five, and how well a child builds it tracks how the adults around her talk about the past with her. Parents who ask open questions and add detail, rather than checking the facts, tend to get children who tell fuller stories about their own lives years later. Seven cards on a wall with her own wrong words under them give that conversation a handle. Read them back, let her correct you, and the week gets filed.

days.safety: Washable non-toxic paint only. Kreston is 11 months and will have a painted palm in his mouth before you have finished pressing it, so his print goes first, while he is calm, with the washcloth in your hand before you start. Keep the pencil off the floor when he is down.
